newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Car buyers benefit from Europe motor industry woes.
newsitem.headline: Car buyers benefit from Europe motor industry woes.

text.p: If you live in Europe, and don't work in the industry, this is a great time to buy a car.
As crowds swarm around on the first public day of the Geneva car show on Thursday, they will find lower prices and juicy deals.
The recent turmoil in the industry shows the industry's malaise.
Jobs are being slashed at Renault SA plants in Belgium and France as well as at Ford Motor Co in Britain, stirring a political storm particularly in Belgium and France.
Prices are tumbling precisely because of these tough trading conditions, and those with secure jobs will find cars more affordable.
Experts say that with the sales outlook for western Europe stagnant, companies will be looking at yet more ways to cut costs including layoffs, plant closures and mergers.

Overcapacity is forcing Europe's mass car manufacturers to cut prices and profit margins to the bone. To keep costs down they must produce as close to capacity as possible. But as there are not enough buyers, they have to fight like ferrets in a sack for sales.
This is leading some car makers to come up with new ideas. If they can't sell a car to you, they'll probably try to get you to rent it.

Peter Cooke, director of the Henley Centre's automotive management group, says the European big six mass car makers -- France's Peugeot and Renault, Italy's Fiat SpA, Ford and General Motors Corp's Opel/Vauxhall, and market leader Volkswagen AG of Germany - are finding it increasingly difficult to make money from selling cars.
Their balance sheets show increasing profits from finance activity, less and less from making cars.
In some depresssed European markets with high unemployment, consumers are unwilling to part with the large sums of money required for a new car.

"In Germany and France where you've high unemployment, the motive to avoid expense is quite high. When you've got 4-1/2 million unemployed (as in Germany), it's a real turnoff, a real feel-bad factor," Cooke said.

"Customers don't want to buy a depreciating asset, so we're starting to see personal contract hire. Americans have been doing it for years. That will develop further with people wanting to have the use of the asset rather than ownership of a depreciating asset," Cooke said.

But whether you are buying or leasing, the balance of power has shifted to consumers in Europe. "Customers have never had it so good," said Peter Schmidt, joint managing director of Britain's Automotive Industry Data.

"It used to be that high cost manufacturers like VW had to charge premium prices compared with Ford, Opel and Fiat. But VW has made huge progress and is using its new found marketing muscle to fight for market share," Schmidt said.
Last year VW, with its Audi, SEAT and Skoda brands, extended its lead as top seller in Europe, raising its market share to 17.2 percent from 1995's 16.8 percent.

"The average German punter can go in to a showroom, and before he's opened his mouth the salesman has already deducted 10 percent," Schmidt said. "Salesmen know that most Europeans have the ability to go over the border into weak currency countries like Italy, or Spain or Portugal and buy via currency fluctuations at significantly lower prices."

The cost cutting drive has created a virtuous circle for the consumer. "VW in particular is getting more efficient, and is passing on some of those savings to customers. Look at the latest Passat -- it's really a thinly disguised Audi A4," said Schmidt.
Volkswagen has cut down the number of basic car platforms to four. It produces the upmarket Audi A4 and the more prosaic VW Passat from the same basic components.

"VW is offering near executive car quality for the price of a (Ford) Mondeo. How can you lose? This is coming across to the public through motoring journals and is really giving the customer more for his money," Schmidt said.
The Geneva car show opened to the public on Thursday and runs until March 16.
New cars on display for the first time include:
-- Audi A6, a mid-size executive saloon competing with BMW 5, Mercedes E class.
-- SEAT Arosa, VW's cutdown Polo and first minicar, competes with Renault Twingo, Ford Ka.
-- Ford Puma, Fiesta-based coupe, competing with Opel Tigra.
-- Mercedes's new sub-Fiesta-sized A class, on show here but not for sale until late this year.
